current_activity: brigade headquarters lands with No. 48 Commando at Saint-Aubin (Nan sector, Juno); landing craft hit mined obstacles
notes: Event date: 6 June 1944, about nine in the morning (Ellis, vol. I, p. 182). Event definition: Brigade headquarters and No. 48 (Royal Marine) Commando, under the 3rd Canadian Division for the assault, land in Nan sector behind the 8th Brigade Group at about nine; three craft carrying brigade headquarters and two with commando troops strike mined obstacles, and the men who reach the shore come under close-range fire from Saint-Aubin before setting off east for Langrune-sur-Mer (Ellis, p. 182; Stacey, p. 77). The brigade's other commandos land in the 3rd British Division sector (Stacey, p. 77; Wikipedia). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 182-183: "Three, carrying headquarters of the 4th Special Service Brigade, and two with troops of the Commando on board, struck mined obstacles"; "came under close-range machine-gun fire from St. Aubin"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 77: "The headquarters of the 4th Special Service Brigade, under Brigadier B. W. Leicester, together with one of its units, No. 48 (Royal Marine) Commando"; p. 77: "were to come under General Keller". Location: Saint-Aubin-sur-Mer, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is Saint-Aubin; headquarters landed on the beach in front of it and No. 48 Commando moved east towards Langrune. Location support: Ellis names Saint-Aubin (p. 182). Commander: Brigadier B. W. Leicester, R.M., commander since the Normandy landings (Ellis, vol. II, p. 118; Stacey, p. 412). Context: Relationship: under the 3rd Canadian Division for the assault (Stacey, p. 77); I Corps as that division's corps; starts = row date (inferred value).

current_activity: takes over the containment of Dunkirk from the 2nd Canadian Division
notes: Event date: 16 September 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 69; Stacey, p. 365). Event definition: On 16 September the 2nd Canadian Division hands over to the brigade the task of containing (masking) Dunkirk and moves to the Antwerp area (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 60 and 69; Stacey, p. 365). The brigade is relieved there on the night of 26-27 September by the 154th Brigade of the 51st Division, to prepare for the Walcheren assault (Stacey, p. 368). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 69: "On September the 16th the 2nd Canadian Infantry Division handed over to the 4th Special Service Brigade the task of containing Dunkirk"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 365: "the 4th Special Service Brigade, as we have seen, assumed responsibility for containing Dunkirk"; p. 368: "On the night of the 26th-27th the 4th Special Service Brigade, being required for the assault on Walcheren then in prospect, was replaced here". Location: Dunkirk, Nord (PL0624) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town; the brigade held the containing line round the fortress, so the precision is 10 km. Location support: Ellis and Stacey name Dunkirk. Commander: Brigadier B. W. Leicester, R.M., commander since the Normandy landings (Ellis, vol. II, p. 118; Stacey, p. 412). Context: Relationship: II Canadian Corps, which held responsibility for Dunkirk until the relief of 26-27 September (Stacey, p. 368); start = row date (inferred value). The 3rd Canadian Division attachment of D-Day is closed the day before (inferred value); the brigade served with the 6th Airborne Division in August (Ellis, vol. I, p. 448), not recorded as a relation.

current_activity: relieved at Dunkirk; withdrawn to an assembly area at De Haan to train for Walcheren
notes: Event date: 27 September 1944 (Wikipedia; Stacey, p. 368: relieved on the night of 26-27 September). Event definition: Relieved at Dunkirk on the night of 26-27 September, the brigade is withdrawn on the 27th to an assembly area at De Haan in Belgium and prepares for the amphibious assault on Walcheren (Wikipedia; Stacey, pp. 368 and 372); Ellis says it trained near Ostend with its headquarters in Bruges (vol. II, p. 118). Event support: three source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 118: "While his men had been training near Ostend, on relief from Dunkirk, his headquarters was in Bruges"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 368: "was replaced here by the 154th Infantry Brigade of the 51st Division"; Wikipedia, 4th Special Service Brigade: "On 27 September the Brigade was withdrawn to an assembly area in De Haan, Belgium". Location: De Haan, West Flanders (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is De Haan; Ellis puts the training near Ostend and the headquarters in Bruges, both within 20 km. Location support: Wikipedia names De Haan. Commander: Brigadier B. W. Leicester, R.M., commander since the Normandy landings (Ellis, vol. II, p. 118; Stacey, p. 412).

current_activity: Infatuate II: assaults Westkapelle through the gap in the dyke; village cleared and battery W 15 taken
notes: Event date: 1 November 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 120-122; Stacey, pp. 412-418: leading troops touched down at 10:10 a.m.). Event definition: The brigade makes the seaborne assault at Westkapelle through the gap the RAF made in the dyke, intending to thrust along the dunes south-east to Flushing and north-east round the coast; with all commandos ashore, Westkapelle village is cleared and battery W 15 taken, and No. 41 Commando sets out for Domburg in the afternoon (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 120-122). At Westkapelle the brigade works directly under II Canadian Corps and, once well ashore, under the 52nd Division (Stacey, p. 412). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 120: "The 4th Special Service Brigade's intention was to capture Westkapelle"; p. 122: "with all Com- mandos ashore, Westkapelle village cleared and the battery (W.15) captured"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 412: "At Westkapelle, where its main body went in, it operated directly under the 2nd Canadian Corps"; p. 412: "Once well ashore, the brigade would come under the 52nd (Lowland) Division". Location: Westkapelle, Zeeland (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the village; the brigade landed at the dyke gap beside it and fanned out along the dunes. Location support: Ellis and Stacey name Westkapelle. Commander: Brigadier B. W. Leicester, R.M., commander since the Normandy landings (Ellis, vol. II, p. 118; Stacey, p. 412).

current_activity: with fighter-bombers and three tanks, takes the last battery and strong-point between Veere and Domburg
notes: Event date: 8 November 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 123: "by the 8th"). Event definition: The last German casemated battery and strong-point on Walcheren, with about 1,000 men between Veere and Domburg, is captured by the 8th by the commandos, supported by fighter-bombers of 84 Group and three surviving assault tanks of the 79th Armoured Division; the only Germans left on Walcheren are then prisoners (Ellis, vol. II, p. 123). Stacey says Domburg itself fell to No. 10 Commando on 3 November (p. 419). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 123: "There remained one casemated battery and strong-point with about 1,000 of the enemy between Veere and Domburg"; "These were captured by the 8th by the Commandos". Location: Domburg, Zeeland (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Domburg, one end of the stretch named; the strong-point lay between Domburg and Veere, so the precision is 5 km. Location support: Ellis places the last strong-point between Veere and Domburg (p. 123). Commander: Brigadier B. W. Leicester, R.M., commander since the Normandy landings (Ellis, vol. II, p. 118; Stacey, p. 412).

current_activity: takes over responsibility for Walcheren and North and South Beveland from the 52nd Division
notes: Event date: end of November 1944 (approximate: Stacey, p. 430, says the 52nd Division left Walcheren at the end of November). Event definition: When the 52nd Division, which had occupied Walcheren, relieves the 4th Canadian Armoured Division at the end of November, the brigade takes over responsibility for Walcheren and North and South Beveland (Stacey, p. 430). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 430: "The 4th Special Service Brigade then assumed responsibility for Walcheren and North and South Beveland". Location: Walcheren island, Zeeland (PL0549) with a precision of 25 km. Location approximate: the point is the island centre; the brigade was responsible for the three islands, so the precision is 25 km. Location support: Stacey names Walcheren and North and South Beveland (p. 430). Commander: Brigadier B. W. Leicester, R.M., commander since the Normandy landings (Ellis, vol. II, p. 118; Stacey, p. 412). Context: Event date is approximate (inferred value: "the end of November", taken as 30 November), hence 0.3. Relationship: the 52nd Division attachment is closed the day before (inferred value).
